then.text: The heather on the hill's flank ripples, slow and wide. Something very big is paying attention.

else.text: You carry ten Stones, and the hill hums back at exactly the right note. The grass round the monument lifts, one long ridge after another, until you realise it's not the hill that's moving.
Seven coils rise out of the bracken, each as wide as a bus. At the top of them, a head the size of a garden shed turns, politely, and regards you.
Whisht, bonny lad, or lass. Haad yer gobs and listen: I've been the subject of that song for six hundred years, and nowt but the tune has improved.
John Lambton fished on a Sunday, tossed me down a well, and went off to the Crusades. I grew. That was the plan, as far as I could tell. Nobody consulted me.
He came back and cut me in pieces, and the pieces could not join up again. I've been working on it. I'm very nearly whole. Care to see if you're worth the trouble?

then.text: The great coils slide away down the hill, one after another, until the last of them is tucked in at your heel like a very large and very pleased dog. The monument seems to approve. The grass, rather unusually, does not move.

else.text: The Worm sinks into the heather, coil on coil, and the hill is a hill again. It will be back on the next Sunday. Worms are very reliable about Sundays.
The grass on Penshaw Hill moves against the wind, in one long, slow coil, then another. Somewhere under the monument, something very large turns over in its sleep.
Mmm. Nine Stones. Close. It's only for ten, that. Come back when the Spirit's in your pocket, and mind your pyjamas on the stairs.
The coil settles. A dog walker in the distance remarks to nobody that the wind's got up.

pen_singer.text: Whisht, lads, haad yer gobs, and Aa'll tell ye all an aaful story! That's how the Lambton Worm song starts. It means: be quiet, and listen.
John Lambton goes fishing on a Sunday, catches a weird little worm, tosses it down a well, and then goes off to the Crusades. This is the story's idea of a plan.

pen_walker.text: You can see the monument for miles. On a clear day you see the sea from the top, and on a foggy day you see the inside of your own hat.
Sundays here are busy. Everyone brings a dog. The dogs bring one another.

pen_kid.text: Seven coils round the hill! And then Sir John cut it in pieces and the bits could not join up. That's the clever part.
I counted the hill's terraces once and got seven. Mum says it's bracken. She is wrong.

pen_volunteer.text: It was meant to be roofed. Nobody had the money, and the roof was dropped, and the columns have stood in the weather since 1844.
I like it better like this. A temple with the sky for a roof can't leak.
